name: Frances Perkins
role: U.S. secretary of labor (1933–1945); New York labour administrator and later Cornell lecturer
summary: Perkins advocated public social insurance, decent labour standards, union bargaining and government responsibility for economic security. Her international labour work and refugee protection accompanied support for women’s participation, while her opposition to the Equal Rights Amendment reflected a preference for protective labour legislation.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Made universal health insurance a condition of accepting the labour secretaryship and continued to identify it as unfinished business.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Demands a national wage floor to raise drastically depressed sweatshop wages and restore decent living standards.

unions-good.rationale: Helped establish workers’ rights to organise and bargain through the National Labor Relations Act.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Advocates enforceable wage, hours and licensing standards to restrain exploitative employers.

cut-welfare.rationale: Rejects treating poverty as individual failure and argues for expanded protection against unemployment, age and illness.

state-harmful.rationale: Praises collective government action against hazards individuals cannot overcome alone.

decide-locally.rationale: Rejects federal dictation of every insurance policy and preserves substantial state discretion within national minimum standards.

gradual-change.rationale: Advocates building social security by degrees, warning that an overambitious first step could discredit reform.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Expanded practical avenues for admitting refugee children and pursued more humane immigration administration.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Advocated expanding the ILO beyond minimum labour standards into international economic planning and policy.

experts-over-public.rationale: Told the committee that it was the duty of Congress and the President, not the experts, to decide what form the programme should take, though she valued the experts' advice. This is about elected bodies versus experts, not the public directly.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Tailors reforms to American conditions and lessons from practical European experience rather than copying one model.

direct-action.rationale: Emphasises legislative investigation and persuasion as the effective route to lasting workplace reform.

taxation-theft.rationale: Defends compulsory payroll taxation to finance public social insurance.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Described relying on divine guidance in making public decisions, alongside empirical investigation.

class-collaboration.rationale: Presents decent standards as serving workers and responsible employers, and favoured negotiated arbitration of the 1934 general strike.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Opposed the ERA because it threatened special legal protections for women workers; supported equality of opportunity rather than identical treatment in every law.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Government should provide social insurance, public health and assistance for vulnerable families.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Helped promote the Philadelphia Declaration’s equal rights to security and opportunity regardless of race, creed or sex.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Makes lower-income households’ living standards central to national economic welfare.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Argues social insurance can stabilise purchasing power and sustain the existing economic system.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Explained that fortunate people should help the poor because of their Christian responsibilities.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Advocates compulsory public old-age insurance with employer and employee contributions, alongside optional annuities.

job-guarantee.rationale: Proposes federal public employment for workers private industry cannot absorb, particularly those already on relief.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Refused to deport labour organiser Harry Bridges without lawful grounds despite political pressure.

social-market-economy.rationale: Defends public insurance and purchasing-power support as necessary to sustain private industry and the existing economic system.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Defended applying immigration law and fair procedures rather than expelling Bridges to satisfy political demands.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Prefers systematic unemployment insurance to haphazard assistance.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Promoted an international declaration coupling economic security with freedom for spiritual development.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Supported enforceable union bargaining rights rather than relying solely on individual employment contracts.

women-suffrage.rationale: Spoke at suffrage rallies and organised women’s electoral participation.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Endorses need-adjusted assistance alongside broader contributory social insurance.

notes:
Her own speeches are distinguished from later historical accounts. The ERA position concerns sex-specific worker protections, not opposition to women voting or holding office. Her refugee initiatives are not treated as support for unlimited entry. Public old-age insurance coexisted with optional annuities. No positions are inferred from religious membership, New Deal affiliation or merely serving in Roosevelt’s Cabinet; unrelated military, ecological and technological questions remain unanswered.

claude-sonnet-5-5 notes: Independent second pass. Full text read: The Roosevelt I Knew (1946) and her January 1935 Ways and Means testimony; her 1914 fire-hazard report. Much of the 1946 memoir records Roosevelt's views, which are not hers and were not used. Not reached: ssa.gov speech pages (HTTP 403), borrow-only archive.org copies of the memoir (the OCR copy used is the scan of the 1946 edition), People at Work (1934), Columbia oral history, Fair Labor Standards Act testimony. The ERA and women's suffrage answers need sources not opened here, so they are null. Themes with answers: economy, government, society, liberty. World and technology: thin or null (the ILO and refugee work are narrower cases than the statements). Sit-down strikes and Bridges are narrower than the direct-action and political-violence statements.
